table.text: The participants were 44 male football players divided into two groups based on their skill level.
To provide a margin of safety beyond the calculated minimum of 31 participants, we recruited 44.
Participants (and parents / guardians where applicable) provided written informed consent to take part in the experiment and were free to withdraw at any time.
Participants were invited to the gymnasium where the experiment took place.

Participants were instructed to perform the task as quickly (i.e., minimizing the time between ball reception and the final pass) and as accurately (i.e., passing in the direction required by the running player's movement) as possible.
First, the participant had to pass the ball to the passing player.
If the run was made to the left or right between the cones, the participant had to pass the ball between the two cones in the direction of the running player.
If the run was made towards the middle, the participant had to pass back to the passing player.
Conversely, the end of the exploratory phase was identified when participants completed their head movement, marked by the return of a clear image in the eyetracker recording.

Most of the players were recruited from a French professional club academy and played in the top French Under-19 Youth league, while others were from the university football team of University of Rouen Normandy.
Participants signed informed consent to take part in the experiment and were free to withdraw at any time.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Studies were not pre-registered. Sample size for Experiment 1 was determined based on an a priori power analysis using G*Power version 3.1.9.6 (Faul et al., 2007). Data were analyzed using R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023), with the following statistical packages: dplyr version 1.1.4 (Wickham et al., 2023) for data manipulation, stringr version 1.5.1 (Wickham, 2023b) for string processing, tidyverse version 2.0.0 (Wickham et al., 2019) for integrated data science tools, effectsize version 1.0.0 (Ben-Shachar et al., 2020) for partial eta squared calculation, forcats version 1.0.0 (Wickham, 2023a) for factor-level handling, and ggplot2 version 3.5.0 (Wickham, 2016) for data visualization. Statistical analyses were conducted either using JASP version 0.18.3 (JASP Team, 2024), or R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023).

An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) to determine the required sample size. The analysis indicated that a minimum of 31 participants would be required to detect an effect size of f² = 0.35 (α = 0.05, 1 -β = 0.80) in our linear mixed model design with skill level (2 levels) × run direction (3 levels) as fixed effects. This effect size corresponds to Cohen's (2013) conventional benchmark for a large effect, and the choice was informed by the literature and by taskrelated considerations. First, the large difference in skill level between our two groups (professional academy and elite youth players compared to novices) was expected to produce a large effect, consistent with the moderate-to-large effect sizes reported in the meta-analysis by Mann et al. (2007). Second, our task is more sport-specific and closer to the participants' domain of expertise than most of the paradigms included in that meta-analysis, which we expected to further increase the magnitude of the group difference. To provide a margin of safety beyond the calculated minimum of 31 participants, we recruited 44. This final sample size corresponds to a sensitivity of f² = 0.24.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Skillful performance requires picking up information at the right time to both accurately perform ongoing action and search for subsequent ones.

The current experiment aimed to compare the visual exploratory activity (VEA) of skilled (n = 23) and novice (n = 21) players in a football-based dual task scenario that required to manage competing visual demands for ball manipulation and environmental scanning.

Skilled players performed the task faster than novices and showed a more proactive VEA: they spent more time looking at cues related to future passing opportunities while novices looked more at cues related to ball reception.
In addition, skilled players made longer scanning movements before receiving the ball, but they did not perform significantly more head movements than novices.
Under mental fatigue, skilled participants preserved their VEA patterns but required longer visual fixations, suggesting a reduced rate of information processing.
These findings suggest that expertise in VEA is characterized by the efficient allocation of visual attention rather than merely its quantity.
Where and When to Look:
We live in a world full of action opportunities, requiring continuous arbitration between alternative courses of action (Cisek & Kalaska, 2010; Pezzulo & Cisek, 2016).
text.formatted: We live in a world full of action opportunities, requiring continuous arbitration between alternative courses of action <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cisek & Kalaska, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Pezzulo & Cisek, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When performing dual taskssuch as receiving an object from one person and passing it to another or driving on a crowded highway while searching for an exit-we must also arbitrate between their competing visual demands, such as looking at the first versus the second person, or at other cars versus traffic signs.
Beyond these everyday activities, most skilled behaviors, such as sports, also involve competing visual demands.

For example, in soccer and basketball, when receiving the ball from a teammate and launching it to another; or in car and motorcycle racing, when driving while also remaining aware of the position and intentions of other drivers.
This prompts the question of what guides visual exploration in such challenging conditions (Hayhoe & Ballard, 2005).
text.formatted: This prompts the question of what guides visual exploration in such challenging conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hayhoe & Ballard, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Decades of research have shown that skilled motor performance relies on internal forward models that support the prediction of action consequences and the planning of accurate movements (Friston et al., 2010; Kawato, 1999; Parr et al., 2022; Wolpert et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Decades of research have shown that skilled motor performance relies on internal forward models that support the prediction of action consequences and the planning of accurate movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Friston et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kawato, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Parr et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Wolpert et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, the predictions generated by these models become increasingly uncertain over time, requiring calibration through external observations.

Various theoretical models propose that it is this uncertainty that drives gaze toward informative locations-gathering observations to reduce the model's uncertainty (Friston et al., 2012; Itti & Baldi, 2009).
text.formatted: Various theoretical models propose that it is this uncertainty that drives gaze toward informative locations-gathering observations to reduce the model's uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Friston et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Itti & Baldi, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, when models generate highly confident predictions, no informationseeking behavior is required, since information that can be predicted with high confidence does not need to be attended to.

Extending this line of thought, it has been proposed that when two internal models are active simultaneously-for example, one predicting the movements of the person handing over an object and the other predicting the movements of the person to whom the object must be passed-the model with greater uncertainty demands more information and thus directs attention to its own most informative location (Rothkopf & Ballard, 2010; Donnarumma et al., 2017).

text.text: For instance, when the movement of the first person is predictable, gaze can shift early to the second person.
In contrast, when the first person's movement is difficult to predict, it must be monitored continuously.
Previous empirical studies have examined the relationship between predictability and gaze dynamics, revealing both anticipatory and information-gain-driven patterns of eye movements.
In one experiment, participants observed an actor reaching for one of two objects (a large and a small one), either with or without hand preshaping (Ambrosini et al., 2015).

text.text: The study revealed that when participants had no clue about the actor's intention-whether to grasp the small or the large object-they simply followed the actor's moving arm with their eyes, as it was the only informative element in the visual scene, until it reached one of the objects.

Conversely, when they could infer the actor's intention from the hand preshape, they made anticipatory saccades to the to-be-grasped object, since the moving hand no longer offered additional information once the goal had been inferred.
A computational model of the task successfully replicated these findings, based on the assumption that information gain guides eye movements (Donnarumma et al., 2017).

text.text: In addition, Sullivan et al. (2012) and Johnson et al. (2014) demonstrated that in dual-task paradigms, where multiple tasks are ongoing simultaneously, the allocation of visual attention is dynamically modulated by the growth of uncertainty across tasks.

text.text: Specifically, the predictive accuracy of the internal model for one task determines the temporal threshold for attentional disengagement, allowing a shift of resources to another task module.
This continuous process enables the minimization of uncertainty across task modules, thereby fulfilling the overarching demands of the dual task.

Another study using virtual reality settings to investigate how participants search for task-relevant objects revealed that gaze behavior is systematically shaped by both the structure of the environment and the observer's task goals, supporting the view that visual exploration is actively controlled to reduce uncertainty in a goal-directed manner (Rothkopf et al., 2007).

text.text: Yet another line of research addressed skilled performance in dynamic tasks and showed that participants often exhibit "justin-time" gaze behavior-fixating on task-relevant elements only at the moment when information is needed to guide ongoing or upcoming actions.

For instance, Ballard et al. (1997) demonstrated that, in a block-copying task, participants looked at each block only immediately before they needed to act upon it, rather than memorizing all block positions in advance.

text.text: A study from Van Andel et al. (2019) proposed that VEA is used for different purposes according to when it occurs relative to action onset.

text.text: More specifically, they proposed that early VEA would aim at searching for the different available opportunities (Exploration for Orientation) whereas late VEA would aim at specifying the selected affordance ("Exploration for Specification").

These two functions were hypothesized to be associated with different VEA patterns, notably regarding the acceleration profile of the head movements as exploring for orientation would aim for discovering the surrounding environment while exploration for specification would aim to fixate a specific location.

A recent eye-tracking study performed by Aksum, Brotangen et al. (2021) suggested that performing VEA between touches of the ball by teammates or when the ball trajectory could be anticipated would be an optimal strategy.

text.text: However, this strategy demands athletes to capture clues to anticipate coming events, based on information pickup before initiating VEA.

To adjust the balance between the two goals when players are about to receive the ball, it could be suggested that players would optimize their VEA to minimize its cost in terms of effort, that is minimizing the time looking away from the ball to control its reception in case of passing and to track the direction of the game, but looking away for a sufficiently long period of time to assess three types of information: namely, the location of free space to move, the availability of a teammate, or the absence of a relevant opportunity.
As emphasized by the coaches interviewed in Eldridge et al. (2023), perceiving such information enables skilled players to make better decisions and manage the rhythm of the game.

text.text: Together, this body of work supports the perspective that visual exploration patterns are not merely reactive responses to salient stimuli, but proactive strategies governed by internal models and shaped by the informational requirements of complex, often overlapping tasks.
Despite these advancements, some open questions remain.

First, it is unclear whether skill level (as a proxy for superior internal models and predictive capabilities) influences the choice of anticipatory versus reactive VEAs in realistic settings, in which multiple tasks pose competing informational demands.

Second, it is unclear whether taxing participants' cognitive processing -for example, by inducing mental fatigue (Hockey, 2011; Kool & Botvinick, 2014) -influences their VEAs or only lower levels of perceptual processing.

text.text: In this study, we performed two experiments that address the above questions.

In the first experiment, skilled and novice soccer players were engaged in a sequential task in which they had to receive the ball from one teammate ("passing player") and then pass it to another teammate in movement ("running player").

This dual task poses competing informational demands, as it requires maintaining information coupling with the ball for controlling its reception, while also visually exploring the movements of the second teammate to prepare passing the ball.

Therefore, it presents an interesting trade-off, since scanning the movements of the running player while receiving the ball affords a better preparation of the passing action but at the cost of losing information about the incoming ball.

We reasoned that since skilled players have better predictive models compared to novice players, which plausibly afford a better prediction of the ball and of the other players, the two groups should show distinct (more anticipatory versus more reactive) VEAs.

Specifically, while receiving the ball, skilled players should look early on at the target necessary to specify the future action (i.e., the running player), whereas novices should look longer at the targets necessary to specify the current receiving action (i.e., the passing player and the ball).
Conversely, novices should initially focus on the ball that they need to receive and look for passing opportunities only after receiving it.
To further increase the uncertainty of the task and prevent participants from relying on a simple binary elimination strategy between left and right, a third, central run direction was introduced.
Runs to the left or right were designed to resemble a teammate's run to offer a passing option in open space.

The central run direction, while still performed by the same teammate throughout the task (i.e., the running player), was conceptually inspired by situations in matchplay where an opponent's press restricts forward passing options, prompting a safe return pass to retain possession rather than risk losing the ball (i.e., passing the ball back to the passing player).

We therefore expected skilled players, who could anticipate this requirement before ball reception based on their anticipatory VEA, to identify the running player's central trajectory earlier than novices and thus perform the pass in the correct direction more rapidly.
Accordingly, we predicted that the performance advantage of skilled over novice players would be even more pronounced in the middle condition than in the left/right conditions.
In the second experiment, skilled players performed the same task under two experimental conditions, with or without mental fatigue.

This design allows us to assess whether mental fatigue impairs strategic aspects of participants' visual processing (e.g., when they collect information about the running player) or only low-level aspects of information processing (e.g., the time required to process useful information).

We reasoned that if mental fatigue decreases the accuracy of the internal models and predictive strategies used by skilled participants, they should adopt the reactive VEAs similar to those used by novices.
Conversely, if mental fatigue only affects low level aspects of participants' information processing, their visual exploration patterns should be similar in the two conditions.

text.text: The participants were 44 male football players divided into two groups based on their skill level.

The skilled group (n = 23) was composed of players aged 17-22 years (MSkilled-Age = 17.87 years, SD = 1.58), with more than 10 years of football experience (MSkilled-YearsOfExperience = 11.04 years, SD = 2.98).
Among skilled players, 16 were right-footed and 7 were left-footed.
All skilled players either competed in the best French youth league or played at a minimum in the 5th French division for senior players.
They were volunteers from the elite group of a professional club academy and from the university football team of the University of Rouen Normandy.

The novice group (n = 21) included players aged 17-30 years (MNovices-Age = 21.95 years, SD = 3.58), with less than 3 years of football experience (MNovices-YearsOfExperience = 1.00 year, SD = 1.38) and played exclusively in recreational leagues.
Among novices, 17 were right-footed and 4 were left-footed.
Novices were volunteer students from the University of Rouen Normandy.
Data for Experiment 1 were collected in 2023.
An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007) to determine the required sample size.

Participants were invited to the gymnasium where the experiment took place.
Upon arrival, they completed a questionnaire providing information about their football profile and vision quality.
Instructions and informed consent forms were provided to the participants in advance of the data collection.

The football task involved 3 participants: the "participant", whose behavior and eye movements were recorded and two teammates, which played the roles of "passing player" and "running player", which were not equipped with mobile eye-tracking systems.
The participant was equipped with the Tobii Pro Glasses 3 mobile eye-tracking system (Tobii AB, 2020) and the calibration procedure was performed, by following Tobii's recommendations.
The task was explained and demonstrated to the three participants by the experimenters.

Participants were instructed to perform the task as quickly (i.e., minimizing the time between ball reception and the final pass) and as accurately (i.e., passing in the direction required by the running player's movement) as possible.
Then, the participant performed a block of 25 trials.
The first 4 were used as warm-up trials and were not analyzed.
The recording quality of the eye-tracker and the point of gaze were checked every 5 trials by asking the participant to look at specific targets in the gymnasium.

If a trial was judged by the experimenters as poorly executed (for example, if the initial pass required a side movement of the participant), it was noted for removal from the analysis and repeated at the end of the block.

Some individuals who played the role of "participants" also subsequently volunteered to play the role of "teammates" (but we did not allow individuals to be teammates before they were participants, in order to ensure that they had no prior exposure to the task when they were "participants").
We developed a dual task that emulated a typical match-play scenario in football and required participants to engage in VEA.

The task involved three participants: the participant in the middle, who wore the mobile eye-tracking device and whose behavior was investigated; the passing player, who was positioned in front of the participant at 6 meters; and the running player, who was positioned behind the participant at 12 meters (see Figure 1).

The direction of the runs was randomized, with an equal number of trials (n = 7) for each of the three directions.
Gaze Behavior.
Participants' gaze behavior was recorded with the Tobii Pro Glasses 3 eye-tracker (Tobii AB, 2020).
This device is a mobile binocular eye-tracker that tracks visual behavior at a sampling rate of 100 Hz using multiple infrared illuminators (8 per eye) and cameras (2 per eye).
It also captures the external scene at 25 Hz using a high-definition camera (1920 x 1080 pixels).
Eye-tracking calibration and data acquisition were conducted using the Tobii Glasses 3 software (Tobii AB, 2019).
Before each participant's block (i.e., the block of 25 trials described above), the eye-tracker was calibrated with the participant standing at arm's length from the calibration target.
The accuracy of the gaze tracking was then verified by asking the participant to fixate again on the target as it was moved within the scene camera's field of view.
If the calibration failed or the point of gaze did not overlap with the target, the procedure was repeated until the gaze location overlapped with the target.
The eye-tracking recordings were subsequently processed using Tobii Pro Lab software (Tobii AB, 2021), applying the "raw" data filter, to perform frame-by-frame mapping of the gaze data.
Performance.
To assess task success and measure performance times, we used the recordings captured by the Tobii Pro Glasses 3 system.
Task response start and end points were annotated using Dartfish video analysis software (Dartfish, 2024).

text.text: We defined the task response start point as the first frame showing the participant's foot contacting the ball following the reception of the return pass from the passing player.
The task response endpoint was marked by the first frame after the participant's final ball contact during the pass to the running player, constituting the task response.
Gaze Behavior.
The visual exploratory activity of the participants was analyzed by measuring the number of performed exploratory phases (scans), their duration, and the gaze dynamics.
In our study, an exploratory phase (scan) was characterized by any head/body movement performed at any point during the trial to collect information about the running player's running direction.
These exploratory phases were identified using external scene video recordings from the eye-tracker.
The start of an exploratory phase was identified when participants initiated head movement, characterized by motion blur in the eyetracker recording due to head displacement.
Conversely, the end of the exploratory phase was identified when participants completed their head movement, marked by the return of a clear image in the eyetracker recording.
Gaze behavior was quantified using two primary metrics: the number of visual fixations per second and the mean fixation duration (ms).

Following the recommendations for dynamic visual tasks (Holmqvist et al., 2011), a visual fixation was defined as a period with a minimum duration of 50ms (i.e. 5 consecutive frames), during which the participant's gaze was directed toward one of three areas of interest: (i) the ball, (ii) the passing player, or (iii) the running player.

text.text: Gaze behavior related to task-relevant AOIs was quantified using dwell time.
Six AOIs were defined: (i) the ball, (ii) the pass area, (iii) the passing player, (iv) the running player, (v) the target area, and (vi) other irrelevant areas of the scene.
Screen captures from the scene camera of the eye-tracker showing the defined AOIs are available as supplementary materials in the OSF repository.
Using these gaze annotations, we analyzed the visual attention patterns of each participant across all trials.

We calculated the average frame-by-frame probability that participants gazed toward cues related to the ball, which included the following AOIs: (i) the ball, (ii) the pass area, and (iii) the passing player.
We also measured the probability that participants gazed toward cues related to the run direction, which included: (iv) the running player and (v) the target area.

For the run direction category, we additionally included the entirety, from the start until the end, of the scans performed as cues related to the run direction, as these scans reflected participants' intentions to seek information about the running player's movement.
To assess the reliability of the coding method, we randomly selected five participants and reanalyzed all their trials three months after the first coding.
Cohen's Kappa showed almost perfect agreement (κ = 0.928) between the two coding sessions (McHugh, 2012).

text.text: Performance.
Task performance was assessed by measuring the accuracy and the time to perform the task.
A trial was considered successful if the participant made a pass in the direction required by the running player's run.
The time to perform the task was defined as the duration between the reception of the pass from the passing player and the participant's final ball contact (i.e., the last pass of the trial).
The effects of participants' skill level and of the direction of the run on task success were assessed using two separate Chi-square tests of independence.
Additionally, we employed linear mixed models (LMMs) to examine the influence of skill level and run direction on task performance and gaze behavior.
Specifically, the participants skill level and the direction of the run were included as fixed effects variables and the participants' ID as random intercepts in the models.
Post-hoc analyses were conducted using Bonferroni-adjusted p-values.
A multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) was performed to analyze the dwell time spent in each area of interest, with skill level as the independent variable.
The dwell time spent in other irrelevant areas of the scene was excluded from the analysis to avoid the linear dependency arising from dwell time percentages summing to 100%.
Some dependency between the remaining AOIs may nevertheless persist, which should be considered a limitation of this analysis.
Effect sizes were reported as Cramer's V for Chi-square tests of independance, partial eta-squared (ηp²) for LMMs, and Wilk's Λ for the MANOVA.
Cohen's d value was calculated for each eye-tracking data point on a period of 2 seconds before and after the reception of the ball to compare the gaze dynamics of skilled players and novices.

The threshold value of 0.5 over a period of more than 5 data points (i.e., 50ms) was chosen as a reflection of a medium effect size (Cohen, 2013) to identify the key time periods where the gaze location differed between the two groups of participants.

Taken together, the results of Experiment 1 show that as expected, skilled participants performed the task faster than novice participants.

Despite both groups showing a similar number of scans, skilled participants showed longer durations of their first scan and looked longer at cues regarding the running player and target area, as opposed to participants that looked longer at the ball and the passing player.
Interestingly, our results reveal that skilled and novice participants used distinct VEAs.
Skilled participants first made an anticipatory scan at cues related to the running players' movement direction before ball reception, then to the incoming ball.
Then, when the running player's direction was to the left or right, skilled participants looked back at the running player just before ball reception, in order to correctly pass the ball to him.
They did not look back at the running player when the direction of the run was to the middle, because they had to pass the ball to the passing player instead.
Furthermore, skilled participants rarely looked back at the ball after its reception.

Conversely, novice participants used a different and more reactive VEA: they focused on the ball almost until its reception and then, when they were about to receive the ball, they looked at the movements of the running player.
Finally, they looked back at the ball shortly after its reception, across all conditions.
In sum, this experiment shows that skilled and novice players adopted distinct VEAs -more anticipatory versus more reactive -during the dual task.

A possible explanation is that skilled participants can focus rapidly on the second task, because their internal model of ball passing permits predicting the ball trajectory with low uncertainty, whereas novice participants have to look at the incoming ball longer in order to reduce their uncertainty -and can only focus on the second task afterwards.

Experiment 1 revealed two distinct (anticipatory versus more reactive) VEAs in skilled and novice players engaged in the dual task football paradigm and suggests that the difference might be due to the different accuracy of internal models and predictive strategies across the two participant groups.
In Experiment 2, we examine whether and how taxing skilled participants' cognitive processing with mental fatigue affects their VEAs in the dual task.

We reasoned that if mental fatigue decreases the accuracy of internal models and predictive strategies used by skilled participants, they should adopt the reactive VEAs that are similar to those used by novices.

Rather, if mental fatigue only disrupts low level perceptual processing, for example, the rate at which information is extracted from the sensory signal, skilled participants should use the same anticipatory strategies identified in Experiment 1 -and the mental fatigue effects should only become apparent in factors related to lower-level visual processing, such as longer durations of visual fixations and scanning movements.

To disambiguate between these two hypotheses, two groups of skilled players performed the same dual task paradigm in football presented in Experiment 1, but in two crossover conditions: either after performing a high-load cognitive task -the Time Load Dual Back -to induce mental fatigue (fatigue condition), or after watching an emotionally neutral documentary as a control condition (control condition).
Thirteen skilled male soccer players (Mage = 19.5 ± 2.1 years, 9 right-footed and 4 left-footed) were recruited for this crossover study; nine of them had also taken part in Experiment 1.

Most of the players were recruited from a French professional club academy and played in the top French Under-19 Youth league, while others were from the university football team of University of Rouen Normandy.
All players had been playing football for at least 10 years.
Participants signed informed consent to take part in the experiment and were free to withdraw at any time.
Three more players withdrew between the different days of data collection due to injuries.
Data for Experiment 2 were collected in 2024.

These keys were covered with distinct colored stickers (White for the "Space" key, Blue for the "1" key, and Green for the "2" key) to avoid any potential conflict between the keyboard key and parity judgments.

The first block started with a stimulus presentation duration of 1200 milliseconds, with an increment of 100 ms between each block, until the accuracy of a block fell below 85%.
Participants took a short break between each block.

Gaze behaviour of participants was recorded using the same mobile binocular eye-tracker device Tobii Pro Glasses 3 (Tobii AB, 2020) as in Experiment 1.

Performance.
We used the recording system in the gym where the dual task in football was performed to measure the duration and success of task performance.

This recording system included three high-definition cameras (1280 x 720 pixels) with a sampling rate of 25 Hz, which allowed the task to be recorded from multiple angles: one camera provided a top-down view, and two cameras provided side views.
Task response start and end frames were accurately annotated using Dartfish video analysis software (version 10, Dartfish, 2024).
We defined, as for Experiment 1, the start frame of the task response as the moment when the participant's foot made contact with the ball after receiving the return pass from the passing player.

The end of the task response was defined as the first frame when the participant's foot clearly no longer touched the ball while making a pass to the running player in the left and right conditions, or to the passing player in the middle condition.

To assess the homogeneity of participants' initial levels of fatigue sensation between the different experimental conditions, we used the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS; Krupp et al., 1989), a validated instrument measuring the impact of fatigue on daily activities over the previous week.

text.text: The evolution of the sensation of mental fatigue was evaluated using both subjective and objective measures.

Subjective assessment was based on a visual analog scale (VAS) administered before and after each experimental condition, i.e. before and after the Time Load Dual Back (TLDB) task, as well as before and after viewing the emotionally neutral documentary (control condition).

This methodology enabled us to verify the similarity of initial mental fatigue states on participants' arrival before each experimental condition, and investigate the evolution of this mental fatigue sensation induced by each condition.
Objective evaluation was based on analysis of performance on the TLDB task, measured by the percentage of correct responses per block of stimuli (30 digits and 30 letters).
As in Experiment 1, we use eye tracking to analyze the average number of visual fixations per second and the mean duration of visual fixations.

As in Experiment 1, visual fixations were defined as periods of at least 50 ms during which participants' gaze was directed toward one of three AOIs: the ball, the passing player, or the running player.

Participants' performance (accuracy, time to perform the task), visual exploratory activity (number of scans, the duration of scans), and gaze behavior related to areas of interest (dwell time) were assessed using the same methods as definitions as in Experiment 1.
Paired-sample t-tests were first conducted to test whether participants arrived at the same state of fatigue between the two conditions.
They were therefore conducted on the number of hours slept and the sleep quality and satisfaction scores for the previous night, measured using items from the St.
Mary questionnaire (Ellis et al., 1981), as well as on the impact of fatigue on daily activities during the last week, measured using the Fatigue Severity Scale (Krupp et al., 1989).

text.text: These paired samples t-tests were also conducted to control the different manipulations on the participants' feeling of mental fatigue.
We conducted a paired samples t-test to compare mental fatigue sensations before each experimental condition (before the cognitive task and before the emotionally neutral documentary).

We also performed a paired samples t-test after each experimental condition, as well as on the differences pre-post each experimental condition to verify a greater induction of mental fatigue sensation during the cognitive task, and therefore a higher mental fatigue sensation after this condition.
We employed a linear mixed model (LMM) to measure the evolution of performance per block of stimuli (30 digits and 30 letters) throughout the cognitive task.
The position of the block relative to the total duration of the task was included as a fixed factor and participant ID as a random intercept in this model.

To assess the effects of mental fatigue and run direction on performance in the football task, we performed Fisher's exact tests, due to the very low number of missed trials, for task accuracy, and we also performed a LMM for time to perform the task.
For this model, the fixed factors included were condition and run direction, and participants' ID was included as a random intercept.
Post-hoc analyses were performed using Bonferroni-adjusted p-values.

Other LMMs were also performed to assess the effect of mental fatigue and run direction on variables related to gaze behaviour, i.e. the number of visual fixations per second, the average duration of visual fixations, and the duration of scans.
In these models, the fixed factors included were condition and run direction, while participants' ID was included as a random intercept.
Post-hoc analyses were performed using Bonferroni-adjusted p-values.

To measure the effects of mental fatigue and run direction on the number of scans performed per trial, we performed a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a Poisson distribution and a logarithmic link.
As with LMMs, we included condition and run direction as fixed factors, and participants' IDs as random intercept.
To analyse the time spent in each AOI (Dwell Time), we performed a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), including condition and run direction as independent variables.
As in Experiment 1, the dwell time spent in other irrelevant areas of the scene was excluded from the analysis.

To compare the visual patterns between the two conditions, we measured Cohen's d value for each eye-tracking frame, over a period extending from 2000 ms before and after the reception of the ball WHERE AND WHEN TO LOOK 29 during the passing player's return pass.

To identify the crucial phases during which the visual patterns differed between the two conditions, we chose to select a period of more than 5 frames (i.e. 50 ms) during which Cohen's d was equal to or higher than 0.5, corresponding to a medium effect size (Cohen, 2013).

Taken together, the results of Experiment 2 show that skilled participants with or without mental fatigue use similar, anticipatory VEAs to address our dual task: i.e. they look at the running player before they receive the ball.
However, participants in the fatigue condition made longer first scans in the fatigue condition.

These results suggest that mental fatigue does not significantly affect the quality of the skilled participants' internal models and predictions, but only lower-level aspects of visual information processing, such as the time they require to extract information during visual scans.

Performing dual tasks in embodied contexts, such as receiving the ball from a teammate and subsequently passing it to another teammate in movement, requires arbitrating between alternative actions with competing visual demands; namely, looking at the incoming ball to ensure a good reception versus scanning the environment to infer the running direction of the teammate to which the ball has to be passed.

By analyzing players' performance and gaze under a dual task football scenario, this study aimed to address how people arbitrate between these two competing demands and the effects of their skill level and mental fatigue on the visual exploratory activities (VEAs) that they adopt.
Our results show key differences in VEA patterns between skilled and novice players in the dual task.
Skilled players demonstrate a longer exploratory phase (800-ms compared to 600-ms for novices, p < .001; see Figure 5A) and more anticipatory patterns of gaze exploration.

text.text: Crucially, they shift their gaze towards the running player's direction at an early stage of the task (approximately 1600-ms before they receive the ball), then look at the passing player, then orient themselves in the direction of the player to which they have to pass the ball shortly before they receive it (see Figure 7).

text.text: We call the VEA of skilled participants "anticipatory" or "prospective", since they appear to prioritize collecting information about their second task (passing the ball) before they complete the first task (receiving the ball).
Novices, by contrast, exhibit longer gaze fixation on ball-related cues related to their first task (Figure 8) and initiate scans towards the running player's direction afterwards (Figure 7).

text.text: We call the VEA of novice participants "reactive", since they appear to prioritize collecting information about their first task (receiving the ball) until they complete it -and about their second task (passing the ball) only afterwards.

A possible explanation of this difference is that novices have poorer internal generative models that generate uncertain predictions about the trajectory and timing of the ball and hence require continuous intake of sensory observations to afford a correct ball reception.
An alternative explanation is that novices require longer visual intake to process information and organize the motor response following each step of this football task (Klostermann et al., 2013).

text.text: Focusing on the middle condition of our scenario, which required passing the ball to the passing player instead of the running player, underscored additional differences in gaze dynamics and task performance between skilled and novice participants.
Skilled players completed the task significantly faster in the middle condition (approximately 450-ms compared to 900-ms in the left and right conditions, p < .001; Figure 2).

text.text: This improvement in efficiency stemmed from the fact that skilled (but not novice) players already knew that they had to pass the ball to the passing player, before receiving it.

It is also worth noting that the exploratory phase of skilled players was approximately 75-ms longer in the middle condition (i.e. about 850-ms compared to 775-ms during the left and right conditions, p < .001; Figure 5A), suggesting that they extended their exploratory activity to ensure the direction of their teammate's movement.

text.text: It should be noted that decision accuracy was extremely high for both groups and across all running direction, suggesting that the task did not discriminate between groups on the basis of decision correctness, but rather on the efficiency with which that decision was performed.
Finally, our results show that skilled players adopted the same anticipatory VEAs even when mentally fatigued.

The effects of mental fatigue were most evident on variables such as the duration of visual fixations and the length of the first scan that are plausibly more related to lower-level visual processing, compared to variables more related to strategic aspects, such as the decision to initiate a scan towards the running player before or after receiving the ball.

This result strongly suggests that mental fatigue does not significantly affect the quality of the skilled participants' internal models and predictions, but only lower-level aspects of their visual information processing.

These results can be understood within a computational framework in which participants facing dual tasks like the one adopted in this study arbitrate between two internal models, one for the receiving task and one for the passing task (Ballard et al., 2013; Friston et al., 2010 Friston et al., , 2017;; Hayhoe & Ballard, 2014; Rothkopf & Ballard, 2010).

text.text: Crucially, both models generate uncertain predictions and pose competing demands to visual attention, as they require collecting information about the incoming ball versus the position of the running player, to resolve their uncertainty.
The key difference between skilled and novice players is the quality of their internal models.

Skilled players can generate confident predictions about the first task (receiving the ball) even with little evidence; hence, they can rapidly turn their attention to the second task, even before the first task is completed.

In contrast, novices have weaker generative models and require more visual feedback to successfully complete the first task -hence they can only turn their attention to the second task after they complete the first.

The observed differences in VEAs between skilled players and novices therefore reflects the fact that resolving uncertainty about one task licenses allocating resources to the other task in an anticipatory manner, as also observed in other visual exploration studies that manipulated uncertainty levels (Ambrosini et al., 2015; Rothkopf et al., 2007; Rothkopf & Ballard, 2010).

text.text: Compared to the previous works, our study specifically addresses a dual task in a real, embodied setting (Experiment 1) and additionally it manipulates participants' mental fatigue (Experiment 2).
The frequency of head turns observed in our first study was significantly lower than that observed in similar tasks, with most trials (72.61%) involving only a single head turn.
This contrasts with McGuckian et al. (2019) study, where all participants (competitive-elite youth players) performed on average about two scans per second.

text.text: This difference may be attributed to the high time pressure of our dual task paradigm and the lower level of uncertainty of the second task, where participants only had to understand the direction of movement of the running player.
In contrast, in the McGuckian et al. (2019) study, participants did not have to control a real ball but had to monitor four screens to identify the available teammate.
text.formatted: In contrast, in the <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">McGuckian et al. (2019)</ref> study, participants did not have to control a real ball but had to monitor four screens to identify the available teammate.

text.text: This distinction underscores the importance of time constraints and task demands in shaping visual exploration patterns.
Summing up, this study proposed a novel decision-making task that effectively enabled to capture the gaze dynamics of football players related to affordance selection.
Our findings revealed distinct visual exploratory patterns between skilled players and novices, highlighting how experience supports the optimization of action through efficient gaze allocation.

Skilled players performed the task faster than novices, skilled players made longer scanning movements before receiving the ball, and showed a more proactive VEA: they spent more time looking at cues related to future passing opportunities, even before completing the first task.
In contrast, novices tended to focus predominantly on ball-related cues rather than looking for what to do next, suggesting a more reactive approach to task execution.

Furthermore, our results revealed that when they are mentally fatigued, skilled participants do not change their VEA, but rather require more looking time, as if the rate of information processing was lowered.
These findings suggest that skilled VEAs may reside in perceiving optimal moments to shift visual attention between taskrelated cues, and not only on the scanning frequency.

Future research could build upon these findings by increasing the time pressure on performers during task completion and manipulating the level of uncertainty in the task modules, potentially further elucidating the efficacy of skilled players' gaze dynamics.
